sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto a larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides a learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of a frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training a separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, a unified generative model with a standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables few-step generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. After a short native-matching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL achieves 2.85 FID using a single sampling step in each stage. Our code repository is at https://github.com/ChengShiest/RevFlow

Figure 1. RevFlow samples on ImageNet 256256. Left: learn faster. After only 5 training epochs, RevFlow-H reaches 1.74 FID with 25 sampling steps per stage. Right: generate faster. After native representation matching, RevFlow-XL reaches 2.85 FID with only 2 NFE in total (one per stage). Both follow the reverse-encoding path: generating from class labels to deep representations, then to shallow representations, before finally decoding to pixels.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, unified generative model with standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables fewstep generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet 256 256, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. After short native-matching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL achieves 2.85 FID using single sampling step in each stage. Our code repository is at github.com/ChengShiest/RevFlow. 1. Introduction Visual encoding and image reconstruction/generation can be viewed as opposite processes. pretrained visual encoder progressively transforms an image into increasingly abstract representations, whereas image reconstruction/generation maps such representations back to concrete visual realizations. In conventional autoencoding [46, 61], the reverse problem is posed as reconstruction: representation is paired with the particular image that produced it, and the decoder is trained to recover that image. Generation poses harder reverse problem. Once abstraction makes different images share similar representations, the inverse becomes underdetermined: representation can correspond to multiple 1 Figure 2. Reconstruction fidelity, few-step generation, fast convergence, and reverse encoding. Left: ImageNet validation reconstructions from SD-VAE, RAE, and RevFlow, with PSNR in parentheses and decoder sizes of 49M, 415M, and 89M. RAE changes the gray hat to red; RevFlow preserves its color. Middle: RAE without matching (1 NFE) and RevFlow-XL with native matching (2 NFE, one per stage). Table 3 reports results without CFG for both adaptations. Right: ImageNet convergence of RevFlow-XL (690M) and RevFlow-H (1.55B) with standard DiT backbones. Far right: RAE generates the encoders endpoint, while RevFlow uses the semantic encoding path to generate deep and then shallow representations before pixel decoding. images rather than fixed target. This distinction becomes especially pronounced for representations pretrained for visual understanding1. Reconstruction-oriented representations, such as VAE latents, retain appearance and spatial detail for faithful recovery, whereas semantic representations learned for visual understanding suppress variations less relevant to semantic discrimination. Such abstraction accelerates generative learning, as exploited by REPA [63] and RAE [66], but leaves more appearance and spatial detail to be generated on the way back to pixels. In RAE-style models, this burden is delegated to separately learned decoder, which is typically around 10 larger than those in conventional latent diffusion [48]; Figure 2 further shows that RAE can reconstruct gray Christmas hat as red. Abstraction therefore shifts, rather than removes, the difficulty: generation in semantic representation space is easier to learn, while decoding becomes more demanding and absorbs an increasing share of generative modeling. Recent methods mitigate this tension by making the generated representation retain more appearance and spatial detail. VA-VAE [61] enriches reconstruction-oriented latents with semantic structure, while RAEv2 [51] combines multiple encoder levels into single target containing both semantic and spatial information. These methods improve the target through alignment or feature aggregation, then learn separate decoding path from that target to pixels. We take different view. Here we define the semantic encoding path as the progression of representations from pixels to abstract semantics that semantic pretraining forms within an encoder. If generation ultimately reverses semantic encoding, why learn separate decoding path back to pixels when the semantic encoding path already connects 1In this paper, unless otherwise specified, encoder refers to frozen pretrained visual representation encoder, such as DINO or CLIP, rather than to reconstruction-oriented VAE encoder. pixels to semantics? We propose to reverse this path itself. Along the semantic encoding path, shallow representations retain more appearance and spatial detail, while deep representations emphasize semantics. The path thus acts like the forward process of diffusion models, which removes information gradually so that generation can recover it through simple reverse steps [21, 52]. Unlike data-agnostic Gaussian corruption, which removes information roughly by spatial frequency [47], the encoder removes it in learned order: appearance and spatial detail first, semantics last [1, 38]. Its reverse resolves semantics first, from deep representations that largely reveal the class, leaving representation learning, main bottleneck of diffusion training [63], to the pretrained encoder. Directly predicting clean shallow features from class label faces an uninformative conditional mean and wide residual variance, forcing stiff jumps onto dispersed clean Dirac targets rather than smooth score refinement. Reversing the path keeps training smooth: the deep stage first models lower-variance semantic space, and its output then provides spatial mean guidance that leaves only narrow residual variance for the shallow stage (Appendix A, Sec. 4.3). This suggests different principle: intermediate representations along the semantic encoding path should serve as successive generation targets, defining how generation unfolds. Generating each target, from the class label or from the next deeper representation on the path, forms stage. How to learn stages that differ in conditions and representation spaces within one model, however, remains open. We propose RevFlow (generation as reverse encoding), which carries out multiple stages of generation along the reversed semantic encoding path with single Transformer backbone. The generation targets of all stages are representations of the same image along the path. Generation proceeds from class labels to deep semantic representations, then shallow representations, and finally pixels. Sharing backbone across stages requires accommodating different 2 conditions and addressing optimization interference across representation spaces. We therefore introduce HyC-DiT, which adapts standard DiT [42] in both architecture and training: global class conditioning is used in the first stage and spatial feature conditioning in the second, while cleantarget prediction enables effective weight sharing across stages. Crucially, the deep-to-shallow stage models appearance and spatial detail before pixel decoding, reducing the generative modeling burden on the decoder. The complete pipeline pairs lightweight decoder with better generation and reconstruction. Beyond reverse encoding, we study native distribution matching for few-step adaptation of semantic representation generators. Existing methods such as FD-loss [59] and representation distribution matching [15] improve fewstep generation by aligning generated and real samples in pretrained feature space, but conventional VAE-based generators typically need to decode latents into images and re-encode them for matching. Generating encoder representations allows native matching without this decodeencode loop. Native matching (NM) improves both single-stage RAE and two-stage RevFlow, demonstrating applicability beyond our reverse-encoding architecture. On class-conditional ImageNet 256256, RevFlow with standard DiT backbone reaches 1.96 FID with 690M parameters and 1.74 FID with 1.55B parameters after only 5 training epochs. For reconstruction, RevFlow achieves 30.25 dB PSNR with an 89M decoder, compared with 18.09 dB using the 415M RAE decoder. After short nativematching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL reaches 2.85 FID using one sampling step per stage and no CFG. Our contributions are: We introduce generation as reverse encoding, modeling the inverse of representation encoding as generative process that reverses the semantic encoding path of frozen encoder from deep to shallow representations. We develop HyC-DiT, unified generative model that learns all stages of the reversed path with one shared Transformer backbone. It injects the class label as global condition and the deep representation as spatial condition through per-token AdaLN. Clean-target prediction avoids the degradation that velocity prediction suffers under sharing, matching separate generators with about half the parameters. We show that pretrained semantic representations can serve as both generation targets and native distributionmatching spaces. Native matching enables few-step adaptation in both single-stage RAE and two-stage RevFlow without pixel decoding or re-encoding. We provide fast-converging training recipe that achieves 1.96/1.74 FID with standard DiT backbones on ImageNet 256 256 after only five epochs, making high-quality generative modeling more accessible for rapid experimentation. 2. Related Work Target spaces for generation. Diffusion and flow models [2, 21, 3537, 42, 53] are trained either in pixel space [12, 23, 32] or in the latents of reconstruction-trained tokenizers [14, 29, 48, 56]. Recent work brings in semantics from pretrained encoders: VA-VAE [61] and REPA [63] align VAE latents or diffusion hidden states with frozen encoder features, REPAE [30] tunes the VAE end to end, and other tokenizers are designed for generation [60, 64]. RAE [66] generates finallayer encoder features directly, and RAEv2 [51] fuses several layers into one latent. All of them generate single target and leave the rest to separately learned decoder, which absorbs more of the synthesis as the target becomes more abstract. RevFlow instead distributes generation across successive levels of the encoder hierarchy. Inverting visual representations. Feature inversion [13, 38] shows that deeper layers become increasingly invariant, retaining semantics while losing appearance and spatial detail; pretrained Vision Transformers [7, 20, 39, 50] follow similar trend. In our ImageNet retrieval examples, shallow features match color and texture, while deep features more often retrieve images of the same class. Such inversions, like autoencoder and RAE decoders, are deterministic regressions. Because encoding is many-to-one, RevFlow models each inversion step generatively and uses deterministic pixel decoding only at shallow level that retains image detail. Multi-stage and representation-conditioned generation. Coarse-to-fine generators decompose synthesis across resolutions [19, 22, 27, 46, 55]. Others first generate compact representation before synthesizing the image: unCLIP [45] samples CLIP embeddings, RCG [33] generates self-supervised representations, W"urstchen [43] generates compressed semantic latent, and Latent Forcing [3] denoises features ahead of pixels. In these methods, the representation conditions generation in another space; in RevFlow, successive targets are paired features from single frozen encoder, each stage reverses one segment of the encoding path, and all stages share common backbone. For spatial conditioning, HyC-DiT follows spatially adaptive normalization [41] rather than using auxiliary control branches [65], computing adaLN-Zero parameters on per-token basis. Few-step generation and distribution matching. Few-step generators can be obtained through distillation [49, 62], consistency training [54], or average-velocity modeling [16]. Generators can also be trained by matching distributions in fixed feature spaces, from maximum mean discrepancy [18, 34] to recent objectives defined on pretrained representations [11, 15, 59]. For latent-space generators, such representation-based matching requires decoding generated latents to pixels and re-encoding them into the matching space; RevFlow instead generates encoder representations 3 directly and matches them natively. 3. RevFlow: Generation as Reverse Encoding frozen semantic encoder maps an image to representations hℓ = ℓ(x) along the semantic encoding path. Deep representations emphasize semantics, while shallow representations retain more appearance and spatial detail. RevFlow divides the reversed path into multiple stages, generating deep and then shallow representations before pixel decoding (Figure 4a). We address three design questions: which representation levels define the generation targets (Sec. 3.1); how unified model shares its Transformer backbone across stages through suitable conditioning and prediction parameterization (Secs. 3.23.3); and how native matching enables one-step sampling per stage (Sec. 3.4). 3.1. Constructing the Reverse-encoding Path Mean guidance and variance reduction. Unlike diffusion, which reverses fixed corruption [4, 47], RevFlow reverses the semantic encoding path, whose order of information removal is formed by semantic pretraining. In clean-target flow matching on at = (1 t)a + tϵ, decomposing clean target = E[au] + separates mean regression E[au] from residual denoising E[rat, u], whose input gradient is 1t t2 Cov(rat, u) (Prop. 1 in Appendix A). Directly predicting shallow representation hM from class label faces an uninformative mean and wide residual variance (hM y), averaging out detail at high noise and forcing stiff Dirac jumps as 0. Reversing the path keeps training smooth: Stage 1 first predicts deep representation hL in lowervariance semantic space, and hL then supplies spatial mean guidance E[hM hL] so Stage 2 refines narrow residual (hM hL) before low-variance pixel decoding [6]  (Fig. 2)  . Params counts pixel-decoder parameters; PSNR measures ImageNet validation reconstruction. 4.3. Ablation studies Table 4 examines generation paths (a), condition injection (b), condition noise (c), and prediction targets (d). Generation path. Table 4(a) compares three paths with the same DINOv3-L encoder, DiT-XL configuration, cleantarget prediction, and five-epoch training recipe. All use 89M pixel decoders and 50 total sampling steps under the common guidance protocol. Deep-only generation gives 2.65 FID and 19.87 dB reconstruction PSNR. Shallow-only generation retains 30.25 dB PSNR but yields 15.94 FID. RevFlow reduces FID to 1.96 with the same shallow target and decoder. RevFlow achieves both high-quality generation and faithful reconstruction, validating the effectiveness of its deep-to-shallow generation path. Replacing the shallow target with SD-VAE latents gives 2.94 FID; adding third stage through layer 16 gives 2.51 FID. Both underperform the default path. Condition injection. Table 4(b) evaluates additional pooled context tokens and the Transformer blocks at which spatial conditioning is applied. Adding pooled context tokens gives 2.02 FID, providing no improvement over 1.96. Restricting spatial injection to layers 1/7/14/21 gives 1.96 FID, matching the default; restricting it to the first layer gives 2.03. Condition noise. During training, Stage 2 receives deep representations extracted from real images; during sampling, it receives the deep representations generated by Stage 1. Removing condition noise increases FID from 1.96 to 2.10 (Table 4(c)), supporting its use in the current recipe. Target layers. An additional shallow-depth study scans shallow targets in DINOv3-S with the deep target fixed at L12 and an 87.12M-parameter decoder. Moving the shallow target from L1 to L3 and L5 improves FID from 4.36 to 3.14 and 2.69, while reconstruction PSNR decreases from 30.19 to 28.32 and 25.48 dB. This illustrates the trade-off between generation quality and reconstruction fidelity when selecting the shallow target. 4.4. Text-to-image generation Setup and baseline. For text-to-image generation at 512 512, embeddings from frozen Flan-T5 encoder [10] replace the class condition in the first stage; the subsequent stage remains conditioned on the generated deep representation. Because published methods use different datasets, we reproduce RAE under our training setup and compare both methods at the same resolution from 5k to 35k iterations. Text-to-image benchmarks. Overall GenEval [17] and DPG-Bench [25] scores. Res.: evaluation resolution. Figure 6. Text-to-image convergence. GenEval is reported as percentage. Markers show measured checkpoints. Dashed lines mark RAEs best recorded scores. Results and convergence. RevFlow outperforms the reproduced RAE at every evaluated checkpoint on both benchmarks  (Fig. 6)  . At 35k iterations, it reaches 77.54% on GenEval and 81.55 on DPG-Bench, improving over RAE by 3.65 and 4.04 points. Both scores still rise from 30k to 35k (from 76.25% and 80.09), suggesting gains from longer training. 8 5. Conclusion RevFlow models the reverse of frozen encoder hierarchy as successive generative transitions, improving convergence and reconstruction with Transformer backbone shared across stages and lightweight pixel decoder. Clean-target prediction enables effective parameter sharing, while native representation matching supports one-step generation per stage without pixel decoding and re-encoding during adaptation. These results establish encoder hierarchies as useful structure for organizing image generation.
